title: Just war
hook: Augustine and Aquinas set limits on war: just cause, last resort, protect civilians

segments.voice: Yesterday, conscience: David in the cave, and a corner of cloth. Your line was the inner voice. What did it say when you listened? Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

Crowds have come out to the Jordan River to hear John the Baptist, and he's not gentle with them. Group after group asks him the same thing: what shall we do? Then some soldiers step forward. Men who carry swords for a living, under Roman rule. They ask too. What shall we do? In the King James words, John answers: "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." He doesn't tell them to put down the sword. He doesn't bless whatever they do with it either. He draws lines around it. Today: just war.

War is a hard subject in the Bible itself. The prophet Isaiah longed for the day when "they shall beat their swords into plowshares," and "nation shall not lift up sword against nation." In the garden, when one of his followers drew a sword, Jesus told him that "all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." And yet nations go to war, and Christians live in those nations, serve in their armies, and lead some of them. So some Christian teachers asked a hard question: if war comes, can it ever be right, and if so, under what limits? Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, wrote to a Roman general about how a soldier could please God. His answer, in short, was that war may only be waged for the sake of peace, never for its own sake. Elsewhere he named what makes war evil: love of cruelty, and a lust for power. Much later Thomas Aquinas put conditions on it: it must be declared by a rightful authority, for a just cause, and with a right intention, aiming at good and away from evil. Later teachers built on them, adding that war must be a last resort and that people who aren't fighting must be protected. Together these became what's called just war teaching. Notice what it is and isn't. It isn't a cheer for war. It's a fence around it. Its rules are reasons not to fight, or limits on how to fight. Not every Christian accepts it; tomorrow we meet churches that refuse war altogether. And looking back over this week: open hands, eating with thanks, people not things, mercy with hands, mercy with words, the inner voice, and now limits on war itself.

Here's the practice: pray for leaders deciding on war, or simply hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place where people are fighting right now, or a leader who has to decide whether they will. Picture the room where those choices get made, and the people far away who will live with them. The first letter to Timothy asks for prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority." If you pray, you can do that now, in your own words. If not, simply hold them, and the people under them, in your attention. The bell holds the time.
Just war. Christian teaching that sets limits on war: a just cause, rightful authority, right intention, last resort, and protection for those not fighting.
Your line: war has limits. Today, when you hear news of a war, notice the people who aren't fighting, and hold them for one breath. Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching and some Protestant and Orthodox thinkers use just war criteria to judge when force may be used and how it must be limited, while the historic peace churches reject war altogether; some churches include prayers for those in authority in their services.

fork.reveal: John draws lines around a soldier's work: no violence, no false accusations, no grabbing for more. Christians read his answer in different ways.

original.note: Latin: just war, the name used for this teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: just war means Christians think war is fine.
what it means: limits on war: only for peace, with rightful authority, a just cause, right intention, as a last resort, sparing those not fighting.
what a scholar hears: Augustine's letter to a Roman general, Aquinas's conditions in the Summa, and later teachers adding last resort and civilian protection.

notes: The index hook credits Augustine and Aquinas with 'last resort' and 'protect civilians'; those criteria were developed by later writers (e.g. Vitoria, Grotius). The script attributes them to 'later teachers'. Owner may want the index hook adjusted.

Augustine is paraphrased from Letter 189 to Boniface ('we go to war that we may have peace') and Contra Faustum 22.74 (love of cruelty, lust of power); not quoted. Confirm. 'A bishop in North Africa' and 'a Roman general' are descriptive; confirm.
Aquinas's conditions (ST II-II q.40 a.1: authority of the sovereign, just cause, right intention) are paraphrased; no count is spoken. Confirm.
'Much later' is a vague time marker; cut if the claims rule wants no dates at all.
'Its rules are reasons not to fight, or limits on how to fight' is an interpretive summary; confirm or soften.
Matthew 26:52 is used here; tomorrow (day 1212) uses Matthew 5:39, so the peace churches' main text is left for tomorrow.
